extracted.intended_audience: Judge Advocates, military disbursing officers, government accountants and attorneys handling public funds
extracted.subtask_short: public money and disbursing officer rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards defining what constitutes 'public money' in military/federal contexts and the duties, liabilities, and procedures applicable to disbursing officers (paymasters, quartermasters, etc.). Includes case-based illustrations and statutory interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funds received for privileges and facilities and sales of public property are public money
rubrics_metrics.description: The various funds received at military posts, reservations, or otherwise as compensation for public property occupied, sold, or allowed to be used or appropriated, or for labor furnished, or privileges or facilities conceded (e.g., rents of fisheries, fallen timber, surplus lumber, manure, metallic cartridge shells, grazing privileges, brickyard privileges, quarrying privileges, cutting ice, repairs to wagons, shoeing of teams, tolls) are public money of the United States and must be accounted for to the Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proceeds cannot be legally retained as a local 'slush fund' or used for the post/command's benefit; disposition to the Treasury is required (citing sections 3617 and 3618, and multiple Comptroller opinions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funds received as damages are public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received from private parties as amercements or damages (e.g., sums exacted from contractors for damage/loss caused to the United States) are public money of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to account for such sums as public money can render an officer liable for embezzlement (cases cited: P. 52, 137; C. 2527, C. 29402).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funds received for use of a public dry dock are public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts collected as compensation for the use of a public dry dock are public money and, absent statutory authority, cannot be expended without appropriation by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Des Moines Dry Dock under act of Aug 2, 1882 — collections had to be deposited to Treasury (P. 39, 395, Mar. 13, 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funds received for use of a portion of waterfront of a reservation are public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent or compensation for use of portions of the water front of military reservations (e.g., for fish traps) is public money and must be accounted for as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such funds cannot be turned into local mess funds or otherwise retained (P. 40, 73, Mar. 27, 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Money used in an attempted bribe and subsequently seized is public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Money offered as a bribe to a government employee that comes into possession of a government official must be deposited in the Treasury as public money under section 3617.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Comptroller opinions (C. 11082 Aug. 21, 1901 and Aug. 14, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Money received from an applicant for enlistment who declined is public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Money deposited with a recruiting officer by an applicant for enlistment who later declines to enlist should be turned into the Treasury under section 3617.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific case: C. 12780, June 27, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpended portion of prison fund turned over to Department of Justice is public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a military prison is turned over to the Department of Justice, the unexpended portion of the prison fund must be covered into the United States Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under section 3618.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Fort Leavenworth prison funds (C. 1481, June 25, 1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: Money received as compensation to soldiers for private work done is not public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Money received by a government official from a private citizen as compensation to soldiers for private work (outside military duty) is not public money and should be treated as a private transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: funds paid to soldiers for private work were turned over to the soldiers rather than deposited to Treasury (C. 29225, Nov. 9, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Money received by Army officers acting as customs collectors during occupation not to be accounted as U.S. funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Funds collected by Army officers as customs collectors under military government (e.g., in Puerto Rico) that are transferred and expended under control of the military commander do not form part of Congressional appropriations and should not be taken up on disbursing officers' accounts with appropriation funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 5464, Dec. 12, 1898; distinguishes funds under military control from congressional appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeds of sale of empty packages and certain supplies: accounting depends on title transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Where packages (barrels, boxes, crates) and other waste products are sold, whether proceeds must be turned into the Treasury depends on whether title to the package passed with issuance of the contents. If title did not pass, the property should be accounted for; if title passed and sale was by the holder, proceeds need not be turned into the Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Army Regs. paragraphs and Comptroller opinions govern (C. 22748, Feb. 13, 1908; Apr. 30, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeds of sale of abandoned private property in Gov't storehouse are public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Private property stored in a government storehouse and apparently abandoned (owners unlocatable after prescribed period) may be sold at auction and proceeds deposited with a paymaster as public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 21533, May 21, 1907 and Jan. 31, 1911; allows temporary transfer for historical research in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeds of abandoned civilian clothing of recruits are not public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Where recruits have abandoned civilian clothing to such an extent they are estopped from reclaiming it, commanding officer may collect and sell clothing with proceeds applied to general mess; such proceeds need not be deposited to the Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 22763 Feb. 15, 1908; owner reimbursed if error (C. 27550 Nov. 30, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeds from sale of garbage at post need not be covered into Treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: Money received from sale of garbage (derived principally from company mess waste) may be disposed of as directed by the commanding officer and does not have to be covered into the U.S. Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23876 Jan. 11, 1912; distinguishes garbage proceeds from proceeds of public property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fines paid according to court-martial sentence are public money
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine paid by an Army officer pursuant to a court-martial sentence is public money and should be deposited under section 3617.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money found on an unidentified body on military reservation is public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Money found on the body of an unidentified man washed ashore on a military reservation should be deposited in the Treasury as required by section 3618.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23692, Aug. 4, 1908; where no burial expenses existed, deposit required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of May 1, 1888 (Military Academy) funds limited to incidental sources, not statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'and other incidental sources' in the Military Academy statute is construed to cover incidental sources only and does not embrace funds that statute elsewhere requires to be disposed of differently (e.g., proceeds of condemned property purchased from appropriations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27201, Aug. 31, 1910; statutory construction guidance for special contingent funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: who is a disbursing officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Any officer of the United States 'having any public money intrusted to him for disbursement' is a 'disbursing officer' within the meaning of sections 3620 and 5488, R.S.; medical officers entrusted with monies for disbursement under certain general orders were such disbursing officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 5269, Nov. 7, 1898; includes paymasters, quartermasters, commissaries, medical officers when funds are entrusted for disbursement.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule on disbursing officer responsibility for funds
rubrics_metrics.description: A disbursing officer is responsible for public funds entrusted to him until the funds have been disbursed or the loss can be fixed on another officer or stopped against his pay; loss without fault does not automatically relieve responsibility absent statutory relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (C. 2304 May 19, 1896) and Court of Claims precedents; relief sometimes available via Court of Claims or statutory provisions (sec. 1062, R.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer liable for payments on forged vouchers/checks
rubrics_metrics.description: A disbursing officer who pays out public money on vouchers or transportation requests that are forged generally makes himself personally liable for the amount paid, even if innocent and acting in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government typically holds such officers responsible; officer may sue for indemnity but not require Government prosecution (cases: K. 16, 635 Oct. 25, 1865, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for loss of checks lost in the mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of a government check sent by mail before reaching payee is treated as a loss of public funds; matter may be submitted to Congress for relief of the disbursing officer who drew the check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation practice illustrated (a. 18853 Nov. 23, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for loss during transportation of funds for troop payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where funds are lost while being transported for payment of troops, the disbursing officer remains responsible (unless loss falls under statutory 'expense and risk' of the United States during authorized transport arrangements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts (e.g., Feb. 27, 1893) may allocate risk of loss during transportation to the United States if specifically applicable (C. 2427 July 7, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer liable for payments made 'without due care'
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments made without due care (per Army Regulations paragraph 658/665) will be charged to the disbursing officer; the officer cannot shift blame for lack of care to the certifying officer if the disbursing officer failed to exercise due care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by erroneous voucher computation where the error appeared on the face of the voucher (C. 25340 July 26, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility when sending checks to contractors by mail
rubrics_metrics.description: If checks are made to contractor's order and require indorsement, mailing them at contractor's request does not necessarily impose added risk on Government; measures (blank receipt, witness to mailing) can be used to provide proof of mailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19072 Jan. 20, 1906 — procedural measures recommended (send blank receipt, witness mailing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funds in hands of paymaster/disbursing agent are not subject to attachment by private creditor
rubrics_metrics.description: Funds in possession of a paymaster or other disbursing agent due as pay, salary, or wages cannot be attached in a suit instituted against the payee by a private creditor; such funds are public money in the hands of the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-established principle applied to various agencies; exceptions when funds have been paid to agent/attorney of payee (multiple cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcontractor cannot control disbursement of public funds by lien or injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: A subcontractor has no privity with the United States and cannot, by notice of lien, injunction, or otherwise, control disbursement of public funds due the contractor; the subcontractor must look to the principal contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 20947 Jan. 3, 1912; R. 52, 194 May 19, 1887; injunctive relief against payment by disbursing officer will be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer should pursue remedies in his own name for misappropriated funds
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the usage of military service and general practice under existing laws for an officer charged with disbursement of public funds to pursue, in his own name and representative capacity, the proper legal remedies when such funds are illegally appropriated or withheld by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War is not required to institute such proceedings; diligence in pursuing remedies supports applications for relief from liability (R. 35, 365 May 7, 1874).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer not entitled to credit for collection expenses on certain foreign checks
rubrics_metrics.description: A disbursing officer who deposits a check drawn on a foreign treasurer (e.g., Treasurer of the Philippine Islands) for collection and is charged exchange is not entitled to take credit in his account for that exchange expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3620: draw checks only in favor of person to whom payment is made
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3620, R.S., provides that a disbursing officer having public moneys on deposit in a public depository shall draw for the same only in favor of the persons to whom payment is made; payments on order of a third party to a firm are contrary to statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments made to third parties at someone else's order plainly contravene the statute (P. 53, 239 Apr. 29, 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of April 20, 1874 inspection of disbursements applies only to appropriated moneys
rubrics_metrics.description: The inspection provisions of the Act of April 20, 1874 apply only to disbursements of monies appropriated by Congress, not to other classes of funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reminds that statutory inspection authority is tied to appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on exchange of funds by disbursing officer (section 3651)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3651, R.S., prohibits the exchange of funds by a disbursing officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statutory constraint; citation noted for practice compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government accounts should be kept in United States currency only
rubrics_metrics.description: Government accounts are to be maintained in United States currency only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy position cited without extended elaboration in this chunk (statutory/administrative practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Army regulation deduction for damage does not prevent voluntary payment to disbursing officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 694, Army Regulations, 1910, requiring that damage to public property be deducted from officers' pay does not prevent an officer from voluntarily paying the amount of damage to a disbursing officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page S95 reference; distinguishes compulsory deduction from voluntary payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lease provision allowing lessee to make repairs and deduct cost from rent is legal
rubrics_metrics.description: A lease provision permitting the lessee to make repairs and deduct the cost from the rent of government property is legally valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms permissibility of such contractual term where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeds of sale of condemned property purchased from appropriations governed by Treasury rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings disposing of proceeds from sale of condemned property that were purchased from appropriations must follow section 3618 and related Treasury disposition rules, not be diverted by general incidental-fund language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in Military Academy context (C. 27201 Aug. 31, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage re: proving diligence when depository fails supports relief applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When an authorized depository becomes insolvent, a disbursing officer should file and prove his claim in bankruptcy and prosecute collection; reasonable diligence in such legal measures supports any future application for discharge from liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 35, 365 May 7, 1874 — practical guidance for post-loss conduct to seek relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank refusal to pay payee's check due to attachment is unauthorized
rubrics_metrics.description: When a payee receives a government-issued check on a depositary bank, the bank's refusal to pay on the basis of an attachment against the payee (levied in the bank) is unauthorized; the pay is public money in hands of depositary and payable only to payee or his order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: C. 54, 361 July 19, 1892; protects payees from third-party attachments at depositary level.
